questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presented for STI screening prior to having condomless sex. She had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus. She had a regular male partner and used barrier contraception with condoms. She had two lifetime sexual partners. Physical examination, including the pelvic exam, was unremarkable. Investigations: HIV 4th-generation Ag/Ab negative Rapid RPR reactive 1:4 Urine gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Send a blood sample for dark field microscopy
Treat for late latent syphilis with benzathine penicillin IM in 3 doses at 1 week intervals
Treat for primary syphilis with benzathine penicillin IM stat

questions.explanation: Perform a treponemal antibody test Falsely reactive RPR testing can occur in autoimmune diseases such as SLE. The RPR is based upon antigen synthesized from lecithin, cholesterol, and cardiolipin and reacts with antibodies produced in response to Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum infection. Similar antibodies can be formed in the setting of autoimmune diseases leading to a false-positive RPR. All reactive RPRs should be confirmed with a treponemal-specific test. Repeating an RPR will offer no diagnostic value. Dark field microscopy is not performed on blood samples but rather on specimens collected from chancres. In the absence of active lesions (primary or secondary syphilis) and with the concern for a false-positive result, therapy should be withheld until confirmatory results are available.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q24

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with HIV presents to clinic with a new onset rash. His RPR was 1 : 16 and his FTA-ABS was positive. His RPR was checked 6 months ago and at that time was nonreactive.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?

options.text: Doxycycline – 100 mg PO twice daily for 2 weeks
Penicillin G – 2.4 million units IM, once
Penicillin G – 2.4 million units IM, weekly, for three doses

questions.explanation: Penicillin G - 2.4 million units IM, once This patient has early secondary syphilis, as manifested by the diffuse, morbilliform rash and RPR conversion in less than a 6-month period. The recommended treatment is one IM dose of penicillin G. Doxycycline for 2 weeks or azithromycin can be considered as alternative regimens. Three doses of IM penicillin G would be appropriate for late latent syphilis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q41

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presented to clinic with a “sore” on the shaft of his penis. He had noticed it 3 days earlier while showering. It was not painful. He denied dysuria or penile discharge. He returned from vacation in Panama 2 weeks ago. He reported unprotected sex with two female partners while in Panama. He had no known drug allergies. On examination, there was a well-circumscribed firm lesion, 1 cm in diameter on the shaft of his penis. Laboratory testing was obtained, including HIV fourthgeneration antibody test, urine gonorrhea and chlamydia NAAT , and a syphilis EIA.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Administer benzathine penicillin IM for 3 doses at weekly intervals
Administer single dose of benzathine penicillin IM
Await syphilis screen and send a confirmatory antitreponemal test if positive
Refer to dermatology for further evaluation

questions.explanation: Administer single dose of benzathine penicillin IM Although appropriate testing should be performed, a patient with symptoms or signs of primary or secondary syphilis should be empirically treated at the time of presentation. Note also that syphilis serologic testing (either treponemal or nontreponemal tests) may not be immediately positive in primary syphilis. When suspicion is high, empirically treat (even when tests are negative). 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin is the treatment of choice for both primary and secondary syphilis. Evaluation of lesions for HSV-2 or HSV-1 is appropriate in this situation. However, the lesions are painless and empirical aciclovir is not indicated. Referral to dermatology could be considered if STI work-up and treatment did not result in recovery. (Image from Cox DJ, Ballard RC. Syphilis. In Morse SA, et al., eds. Atlas of Sexually Transmitted Diseases and AIDS. 4th ed. Saunders; 2010.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q11

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man presented with fevers, headache, and myalgia. He had been treated 24 hours earlier with 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin intramuscularly for a diagnosis of secondary syphilis. He reported four male sexual partners in the past 6 months, with inconsistent condom use. On exam, he was diaphoretic, his blood pressure was 96/56 mmHg, heart rate 106 beats/minute, and his temperature was 38.2°C. He had a diffuse macular rash which included the soles of his feet and his palms. There was no meningism. Investigations: Syphilis EIA positive RPR positive 1:128 Specific antitreponemal antibody positive HIV fourth-generation Ag/Ab test failed – please send a repeat
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Inflammatory response to dying spirochetes The patient has developed a Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction after treatment of his syphilis. This syndrome is characterized by release of lipoproteins, cytokines, and immune complexes shortly after treatment. This reaction is characterized by fevers, chills, headaches, and myalgias. NSAIDs are recommended for treatment for these symptoms, and the reactions are usually self-limited.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q12

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presented with an 8-day history of a rash. He was sexually active and had receptive and insertive anal intercourse with 2 male partners in the last 30 days. He had previously had a penile ulcer which had resolved 6 months earlier. On examination there was a diffuse, painless, macular rash involving the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Investigations: Syphilis EIA positive RPR positive at 1:128 Specific antitreponemal antibodies positive. The patient was treated for secondary syphilis.
questions.lead_in: How should the patient’s sexual contacts be managed?

options.text: Advise them to seek care with their healthcare provider
Test for syphilis and treat if positive
Treat presumptively with doxycycline for 2 weeks

questions.explanation: Treat presumptively with benzathine penicillin Persons exposed to patients with primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis should be evaluated clinically and serologically, but those who have had sexual contact with a patient with primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis within 90 days preceding diagnosis should be treated presumptively for early syphilis, even if serologic testing is negative.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q10

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presented with acute vision loss on the left. His eye was not painful. There was no discharge from his eye. He had no past medical history. He reported unprotected sex with 3 male sexual partners in the last 6 months. He had never had an HIV test. On examination there was a posterior uveitis of the left eye. Investigations: Syphilis EIA positive RPR 1:128 FTA-ABS positive HIV test pending
questions.lead_in: What is the next best test?

options.text: Urine nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia

questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture Lumbar puncture (LP) is indicated to evaluate for neurosyphilis if ocular syphilis is present. All patients with ocular syphilis require HIV testing and LP . Neisseria may cause a keratoconjunctivitis and typically has very purulent discharge. Chlamydia may cause conjunctivitis that can progress to keratitis but does not typically cause posterior uveitis. The patient should have pain if the cornea is involved.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q10

questions.question: A woman is seen in your office with an RPR titer of 1:32. Two years earlier, she had a diffuse rash and was treated for syphilis with one intramuscular injection of penicillin. At that time, her RPR was 1:64. Currently, she is asymptomatic and has a normal physical exam.

parts.text: Name 2 reasons the RPR is still positive.
What is one test you would do now, and explain how the result would change your management?

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 reasons RPR remains positive at a lower but persistent titer: (1) serofast state - a proportion of adequately treated patients retain a persistently low positive nontreponemal titer despite cure; (2) reinfection with a new syphilis exposure since treatment.
b) One test now: repeat quantitative RPR in several weeks and compare trend (looking for a further 4-fold rise or fall); a 4-fold rise supports reinfection/treatment failure (retreat +/- consider neurosyphilis workup with CSF exam), a stable or falling titer supports serofast state (no further treatment needed, continued serologic follow-up).

questions.question: 5. a) State the probability of neonatal syphilis in the following two scenarios: i) Chancre, untreated, during pregnancy ii) 1:32 RPR, 14 months before pregnancy, untreated

parts.text: a) State the probability of neonatal syphilis in the two scenarios
b) What is Hutchinson's Triad?
c) Baby is born with neonatal syphilis (CSF is positive, has snuffles). You decide to give Penicillin. Should it be administered IV or IM, and why?
d) What isolation precautions are indicated for this baby?

cohort_answer.text: Chancre untreated during pregnancy: 60-90% (CPS: 70-100% primary syphilis). 1:32 RPR 14mo before pregnancy, untreated (late latent): <10%. Hutchinson's Triad: interstitial keratitis, teeth abnormalities, 8th nerve deafness. Penicillin route: IV ideally, because IM does not penetrate CSF to same degree. Isolation: Routine precautions, unless cutaneous lesions exist then gloves needed

questions.question: Syphilis question- person with remote of hives with penicillin

parts.text: 2 alternative treatments
4 characteristics about classic syphilitic chancre
3 manifestations of tertiary syphilis
3 ways to dx late latent syphilis

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 alternative treatments (remote hives with penicillin, non-severe reaction - can consider desensitization, but alternatives): doxycycline 100 mg PO BID (duration per stage), and ceftriaxone (IM/IV, per stage) - tetracycline is another accepted alternative.
b) 4 features of the classic syphilitic chancre: (1) single, painless ulcer; (2) indurated, clean base; (3) well-demarcated, punched-out edges; (4) non-tender regional lymphadenopathy; heals spontaneously in 3-6 weeks even without treatment.
c) 3 manifestations of tertiary syphilis: (1) gummatous syphilis (destructive granulomatous lesions of skin/bone/viscera); (2) cardiovascular syphilis (aortitis, aortic aneurysm/aortic regurgitation); (3) late neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis, general paresis).
d) 3 ways to diagnose late latent syphilis: (1) positive syphilis serology with no clinical signs/symptoms and no documented negative test within the preceding 12 months (duration >1 year or unknown); (2) history/epidemiologic information excluding exposure/infection within the past year; (3) comparison of current titer with a prior documented titer showing no recent 4-fold rise (arguing against a recent/early infection).

questions.question: A man is diagnosed with primary syphilis. He has a history of an anaphylactic allergy to penicillin from childhood – (2019)

parts.text: A) What are two alternative therapies to penicillin?
B) What are 4 characteristics of a syphilitic chancre?
C) What are 3 diagnostic criteria for late latent syphilis?
D) Name 3 manifestations of tertiary syphilis - must be different organ systems.

cohort_answer.text: Alternatives: Doxycycline; Azithro 2g x1; Ceftriaxone; Desensitization to PCN. Chancre characteristics: Generally non-painful; Spontaneous healing over 3-6 week period regardless of tx; Non-exudative base; Raised, indurated margin; Regional, bilateral LAD; Typically on genitals. Late latent criteria: Asymptomatic; Acquired infection over 1 year ago; Does not meet criteria of documented seroconversion or 4-fold titer increase in previous 12 months, symptoms of primary/secondary syphilis in previous 12 months, or sexual exposure to partner with primary/secondary/early latent syphilis in previous 12 months. Tertiary manifestations: Tabes dorsalis - destruction of dorsal column/root of spinal cord; Gummatous disease of skin (also granulomas of bone, organs); Aortitis

parts.text: List 3 pathogens (genus and species) in which Doxycycline CAN be considered for treatment for genital ulcers.

questions.model_answer: Three genital ulcer pathogens for which doxycycline can be considered: (1) Treponema pallidum (syphilis - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x14 days is an alternative to penicillin). (2) Chlamydia trachomatis (lymphogranuloma venereum - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x14-21 days). (3) Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis/granuloma inguinale - doxycycline for a minimum of 3 weeks or until lesions heal).

questions.question: Mom with secondary syphilis during pregnancy

parts.text: Risk of transmission to the fetus
Four test to do (for mom and fetus)
Drug route and duration for baby
How to treat mom (number of dose)

questions.model_answer:
a) Risk of transmission to fetus with maternal secondary syphilis: very high, approximately 60-100% (secondary syphilis, like primary and early latent, carries the highest transplacental transmission risk).
b) 4 tests: for mother - quantitative nontreponemal test (RPR/VDRL) and treponemal confirmatory test (TPPA/FTA-ABS); for fetus - detailed obstetric ultrasound (looking for hepatomegaly, ascites, hydrops, placentomegaly) and, if indicated, amniotic fluid PCR/dark-field for T. pallidum.
c) Baby's treatment (if congenital syphilis confirmed/presumed): aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV for 10 days (alternative: procaine penicillin G IM daily for 10 days).
d) Mother's treatment for secondary syphilis: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM, single dose.

questions.question: 8) 3 organisms genus and species causing genital ulcer disease that may be treated with doxy

parts.text: 3 organisms genus and species causing genital ulcer disease that may be treated with doxy

questions.model_answer: Three genital ulcer pathogens for which doxycycline can be considered: (1) Treponema pallidum (syphilis - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x14 days is an alternative to penicillin). (2) Chlamydia trachomatis (lymphogranuloma venereum - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x14-21 days). (3) Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis/granuloma inguinale - doxycycline for a minimum of 3 weeks or until lesions heal).

questions.question: Pregnant mother, risk of syphilis transmission to baby if:

parts.text: Chancre on her vulva
Had RPR 1:32 14 months before pregnancy, no follow up no treatment
Baby born with syphilis, LP abnormal - Pen crystalline or benzathine, and why

cohort_answer.text: Chancre on her vulva: The risk of transmission in untreated women is 70-100% with primary or secondary syphilis, 40% with early latent syphilis and 10% in late latent stages in pregnancy. RPR 1:32 14 months before, no follow up: ?late latent so 10%. Baby with abnormal LP: Crystalline has better CNS penetration

questions.question: Secondary Syphilis with penicillin anaphylaxis

parts.text: Provide 3 reasons to LP in non-HIV pt.
Name 2 treatments including the dose.
What is the follow up serology?

cohort_answer.text: LP reasons: Neurologic symptoms present; Inappropriate response to therapy; Any features of tertiary syphilis. Treatments: Penicillin Benzathine 2.4MU IM x1 dose (following desensitization); Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x14 days; CRO 1-2g IM or IV daily for 10-14 days. Follow-up serology: 6 months; expect titre to drop by 8-fold (4 dilutions), e.g. 1:32 to 1:2.

questions.question: Syphilis – CMIA +, RPR -, TPPA +

parts.text: Provide 4 reasons other than false positive.

cohort_answer.text: Other treponemal infection (Bejel, Pinta, Yaws); Late latent syphilis; Prior treatment; Prozone effect.

questions.question: PM Q8. Lady had a rash 2 years ago (generalized, sounds like secondary syphilis), RPR then 1:64, treated with Benzathine Penicillin IM x1, now back, asymptomatic with RPR 1:32 and TPPA (+)

parts.text: a) What are 2 reasons for her positive test?
b) What is one test you could do now which might influence your treatment decision?

cohort_answer.text:
Serofast (expect 16-fold drop at 12 months for secondary syphilis); Re-infection; Persistent infection including neurologic involvement
Lumbar puncture for VDRL (if positive, dictates need for IV treatment; if negative, treat with 3 doses of benzathine penicillin IM for latent disease of unknown duration). If four-fold reduction in RPR and serofast, repeat RPR in 2 weeks to ensure not changing

questions.question: AM 21. Treated for syphilis 2 years ago for RPR 1:64. She had a maculopapular rash. 1 dose of Benz PenG 2 years ago, no f/u serologies. Now presents with RPR 1:32. Treponemal test was positive

parts.text: Name 2 reasons for the positive RPR now. (1)
What test would you do that would change your management? (1)

cohort_answer.text: Reasons: Re-infection; Treatment failure; Neurosyphilis. Test: LP - if neurosyphilis, 14 days IV aqueous Pen G instead of Benzathine Pen.

questions.question: 25. Syphilis

parts.text: Primary syphilis, 2 alternatives to treat (anaphylaxis to PCN)
4 characteristics of classic chancre
3 diagnostic criteria for LL syphilis
3 syndromes of tertiary syphilis

cohort_answer.text: Alternatives: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x14 days; Ceftriaxone 1g IM/IV q24h x14 days. Chancre: begins as papule 1-2cm, non-exudative, raised indurated margins, not painful. LL syphilis criteria: >1 year, asymptomatic, serologic evidence of disease. Tertiary syndromes: Gumma, cardiovascular (aortic), neurologic (tabes dorsalis, general paresis of the insane).

questions.question: Syphilis + CLIA, RPR 1:64 + TPPA with rash treated with PCN IM x1 but lost to f/u, returns 2 yrs later asymptomatic but RPR 1:32.

parts.text: What are two reasons for the positive treponemal test?
What further testing would you do and explain how it would affect your management

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 reasons for a persistently positive treponemal test (TPPA) despite treatment: treponemal tests remain positive for life in most patients regardless of treatment (do not reflect disease activity); this in itself is expected and not abnormal. For the falling-but-still-positive RPR: (1) serofast state after adequate treatment, (2) reinfection.
b) Further testing: repeat quantitative RPR to trend the titer over subsequent weeks/months - a further 4-fold rise suggests reinfection or treatment failure (warranting retreatment and consideration of neurosyphilis workup with LP), whereas a stable/declining titer supports serofast state (no further treatment, continue serologic surveillance).

questions.question: Syphilis titre from 1:64 treated with 1 dose of IM benzathine PCN. Titre down to 1:32.

parts.text: What are 2 reasons for this?
What is 1 further investigation and how will it change your management?

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 reasons for titer decline from 1:64 to 1:32 (less than the expected 4-fold drop): (1) normal/adequate treatment response still in progress - a 4-fold decline is expected by 6-12 months and may simply take more time; (2) serofast state - some patients never achieve a full 4-fold decline despite adequate treatment.
b) Further investigation: repeat quantitative RPR at a further interval (e.g., 3-6 months) to assess for continued decline, stability (serofast), or a 4-fold rise (suggesting reinfection or treatment failure, prompting retreatment and consideration of an LP for neurosyphilis).

questions.question: Pregnant lady with maculopapular rash involving palms and soles at 30 weeks, but skipped all pre-natal care, now delivered a baby. Syphilis serology positive with high RPR titre. Hepatitis B and HIV rapid test were negative.

parts.text: What is risk of transmission to baby in this case
What test do you request for baby to look for signs of congenital syphilis
Baby otherwise ok, has RPR of 1:32, do you treat? If so, what do you treat the baby with? Include drug, route and duration.
What do you treat the mother with?

cohort_answer.text: Risk of transmission: In this case 60-100% for 1st and 2nd degree maternal syphilis. Test for baby: RPR (in reality would also do Syphilis serology EIA/RPR/TPPA, CBC, LP for cell count protein glucose, VDRL, Long bone XR, Ophthalmologic/Audiologic Assessment). Baby treatment: Yes treat - Penicillin G 50,000U/Kg/dose Q12h for the first week then Q8h for three more days (total 10d). Mother treatment: Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM x1

questions.question: You see a woman with HIV infection (CD4 count 560 cells/mm3) presenting with RPR of 1:8. She had a negative RPR 6 months ago. She is asymptomatic and is not pregnant.

parts.text: What stage of syphilis does she have?
How should she be treated (name drug, dose, route, duration)?
If the patient had a penicillin allergy, how should she be treated?

questions.model_answer:
a) Stage of syphilis: early latent syphilis (documented seroconversion from a negative RPR within the past 12 months, asymptomatic).
b) Treatment: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM, single dose.
c) If penicillin-allergic: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 14 days.

questions.question: 27-year old man with chlamydia, gonorrhea and treponemal test positive. His RPR is 1:256, w (NOTE: did not specify location of Chlamydia/gonorrhea infection, or whether patient is MSM etc) per PHAC

parts.text: What 3 drugs would you treat with? Include dose, route, duration
What are 2 reasons for RPR not decreasing 4 fold at 12 months, other than incorrect clinical staging at diagnosis

questions.model_answer:
a) 3 drugs with dose/route/duration: (1) benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM x1 dose for syphilis (assuming early syphilis given the high titer); (2) ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1 dose for gonorrhea; (3) doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x7 days for chlamydia.
b) 2 reasons RPR fails to decline 4-fold by 12 months (other than incorrect staging): (1) HIV coinfection, which can blunt/delay the serologic response to treatment; (2) reinfection with a new syphilis exposure during the follow-up period.
questions.beyond_mandell: PHAC Canadian Guidelines on Sexually Transmitted Infections for treatment doses.

questions.question: Q69 (2023 Day 1). 27 year old male with RPR 1:128 (negative RPR 3 months ago), positive chlamydia and gonorrhea. No specific symptoms mentioned. (HIV/STI)

parts.text: List 3 antibiotics indicated including name, dose, route, and frequency
If RPR not 4 fold decrease give 2 reasons why

cohort_answer.text:
Syphilis: Early (Primary, Secondary, early latent) - Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM x1. Late (Late latent, tertiary) - Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly x3. Neurosyphilis - Crystalline Pen G 4 million units q4h IV x14 days.
Chlamydia: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7 days.
Gonorrhea: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1.
If RPR not 4-fold decrease, 2 reasons: Recurrent infection; Neurosyphilis; Inadequate treatment.

questions.question: You get a call regarding an infant with a normal physical exam, born to mother found to have syphilis late in pregnancy, who was not able to be treated before delivery.

parts.text: What two serologic tests from the mother would you send?
What other FOUR investigations would you order to investigate other than syphilis serology?
Name the treatment for each the mother and the neonate (antibiotic and route, no dose)

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 maternal serologic tests: quantitative nontreponemal test (RPR or VDRL) and a treponemal confirmatory test (TPPA, FTA-ABS, or CLIA/EIA).
b) 4 other infant investigations: (1) long-bone radiographs (looking for periostitis/osteochondritis of congenital syphilis); (2) CBC with differential and platelet count; (3) liver function tests; (4) cerebrospinal fluid analysis (cell count, protein, and CSF-VDRL) - ophthalmologic exam and CXR are also acceptable alternatives.
c) Treatment: mother - benzathine penicillin G, intramuscular route; neonate - aqueous crystalline penicillin G, intravenous route (or procaine penicillin G intramuscular route).

questions.question:
Q14 (2014)
Neurosyphilis

parts.text: 3 indications for an LP
B) 2 indications that the patient is failing treatment for neurosyphilis
C) How do you tx an HIV+ patient with neurosyphilis (state 2 key principles) who has an anaphylactic penicillin allergy?

cohort_answer.text:
Indications for LP (CID 2009): Presence of neurologic or ophthalmic symptoms or signs; Congenital syphilis; Previously treated patients who fail to achieve adequate serologic response to treatment; Tertiary syphilis (controversial, but in HIVinfo guidelines); HIV patients with neurologic symptoms/signs, late latent syphilis, RPR ≥1:32, CD4<350 cells/µL or treated syphilis with suboptimal decline in VDRL/RPR titre (some experts recommend CSF exam in all HIV-infected individuals); some experts recommend CSF exam in all patients with RPR ≥1:32.

B) Clinical progression; Increase in RPR/VDRL by ≥2 dilutions; CSF pleocytosis fails to resolve (should occur over 6 months, can take up to 2 years to normalize). CSF VDRL titre should decline 4x in 1 year but can take years to revert to negative; persistently high CSF-VDRL titre after tx may warrant retreatment. If CSF pleocytosis and elevated protein have resolved and serum VDRL has not risen, additional tx is unlikely beneficial.

C) Confirm penicillin allergy (history and allergist referral); desensitization to be attempted; consider alternative tx with Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h x14 days (or potentially Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x28 days, but not for neurosyphilis).

questions.question:
Q31 (2007)
A man presents with optic neuritis. VDRL and FTA-ABS are positive

parts.text: A) Additional investigations
B) Treatment for late latent syphilis?
C) Treatment for tertiary syphilis?

cohort_answer.text:
A) Persons with syphilis and symptoms/signs suggesting neurologic disease (e.g., cranial nerve dysfunction, meningitis, stroke, hearing loss) or ophthalmic disease with cranial nerve involvement (e.g., uveitis, iritis, neuroretinitis, optic neuritis) should have evaluation including: CSF analysis, ocular slit-lamp ophthalmologic examination, and otologic examination. Other screening: STI, HIV.

B) Benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg IM up to adult dose of 2.4 million units IM q weekly x3 doses (vs early latent syphilis treated with only 1 dose of benzathine penicillin).

C) Tertiary syphilis with normal neurologic exam: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM q weekly x3 doses (7.2 million units total). Neurosyphilis and ocular syphilis: Penicillin G 3-4 million units IV q4h x10-14 days (18-24 million units total).

questions.question: HIV+ patient with positive syphilis serology, develops neurological sequelae. NOT for ocular symptoms, it should be neurological symptoms.

parts.text: 3 indications for LP. 3 things to ask for on CSF?

cohort_answer.text: Indications for LP: any patient diagnosed with syphilis with clinical signs/symptoms suggesting neurologic, ocular, or otic involvement; patients with syphilis without appropriate clinical/serologic response to initial therapy; asymptomatic patients with HIV diagnosed with syphilis with RPR>1:32 or CD4<350 (controversial); neonatal syphilis workup. CSF investigations: VDRL (screening, not sensitive but highly specific; may be falsely positive with blood-tinged CSF, malaria, lupus, hepatitis A, HIV, lyme, mono, pregnancy); if VDRL reactive confirm with TPPA; if non-reactive test FTA-ABS; Cell count >20 cells/microL supports diagnosis in HIV+ patients (>5 in HIV-negative)

questions.question: HIV+ patient with positive syphilis serology, develops neurological sequelae. Patient has hives to cefixime.

parts.text: How do you manage if patient has neurosyphilis?

cohort_answer.text: Desensitize patient; IV penicillin G 3-4 million units q4h for 10-14 days; IF unable to desensitize: Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily d1-14 days

questions.question: HIV+ patient with positive syphilis serology, develops neurological sequelae.

parts.text: 2 ways to determine treatment failure

cohort_answer.text: Recurrence or persistence of symptoms; Lack of a fourfold decrease in nontreponemal test titers at 12 months (early syphilis) or 24 months (late/latent syphilis of unknown duration); Sustained (>2 weeks) fourfold increase in nontreponemal test titers at any time after treatment; Abnormal CSF 2 years after therapy for neurosyphilis

questions.question: Scenario with woman who had intercourse with patient now diagnosed with secondary syphilis. What to do (investigations and/or treatment) in each scenario?

parts.text: A) Not pregnant, no allergies

cohort_answer.text: Screen sexual partners going back 6 months from dx of secondary syphilis. If positive, requires treatment

questions.question: Scenario with woman who had intercourse with patient now diagnosed with secondary syphilis. What to do (investigations and/or treatment) in each scenario?

parts.text: C) Positive RPR at 1:8, pregnant at 36 weeks and anaphylaxis to penicillin

cohort_answer.text: Needs admission for desensitization, then receiving IV penicillin G

questions.question: Scenario with woman who had intercourse with patient now diagnosed with secondary syphilis. What to do (investigations and/or treatment) in each scenario?

parts.text: D) Positive RPR, treated at 28 weeks. What to do for baby?

cohort_answer.text: Risk of transmission depends on stage (1° - 100%, 2° - 70%, early latent - 40%, late latent - <10%) and stage of pregnancy (can occur as early as 9 weeks, uncommon before 20 weeks). Mom should have detailed fetal ultrasound; if evidence of congenital syphilis treat with fetal monitoring in place. If mom adequately treated >4 weeks before delivery with fall in RPR: baseline assessment for signs of congenital syphilis, check serology at 0,3,6,18 mo, but do not treat. If treponemes identified on infant exam, or RPR 4x higher than mom, or 4x rise, or findings compatible with congenital syphilis at any age, or reactive NTT/TT at 12mo or reactive TTx2 at 18mo: initiate treatment plus long-bone radiographs, CBC+diff, CSF sampling (cell count, diff, glucose, protein, VDRL), with low threshold for ophtho/audiology assessment

questions.question: +CLIA, RPR 1:64, TPPA+ with rash treated with Penicillin IM x1 but lost to follow up. Returns 2 years later asymptomatic but RPR 1:32

parts.text: What are 2 reasons for the positive (non)treponemal test?

cohort_answer.text: Treatment failure/inadequate response (consider late latent or neurosyphilis); Re-infection; Expect titres to reduce 4 fold/2 titre classes

questions.question: +CLIA, RPR 1:64, TPPA+ with rash treated with Penicillin IM x1 but lost to follow up. Returns 2 years later asymptomatic but RPR 1:32

parts.text: What further testing should you do and explain how it would affect your management?

cohort_answer.text: HIV serology; LP to rule out neurosyphilis

questions.question: Mom is RPR negative, treponemal test +, treated with 3 doses penicillin x3 weeks. Retested prior to delivery, now RPR 1:16

parts.text: Most likely explanation for negative assay initially?

cohort_answer.text: They are asking why RPR (non-trep) was negative initially, trep positive: Old infection - may have been treated, may not have been treated (RPR will start to fall on its own with enough time); Early in new infection RPR can be negative while trep positive; Prozone effect (so much syphilis Ab that it messes with the testing mechanism); Can have false positive RPR in pregnancy. (Also noted: for patients with history of treated syphilis, presence of positive nontreponemal test indicates new infection, evolving response to recent treatment, treatment failure, or serofast state)

questions.question: Mom is RPR negative, treponemal test +, treated with 3 doses penicillin x3 weeks. Retested prior to delivery, now RPR 1:16

parts.text: What to do for baby?

cohort_answer.text: Do assessment as above then...

questions.question: Mom is RPR negative, treponemal test +, treated with 3 doses penicillin x3 weeks. Retested prior to delivery, now RPR 1:16

parts.text: 4 radiographic or lab findings

cohort_answer.text: Lab findings: CBC - DAT negative hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis or leukopenia; CSF pleocytosis (>25 WBC/microL infants <1 month), elevated CSF protein; Reactive serology, CSF VDRL reactive; Elevated transaminases; Increase in direct and indirect hyperbilirubinemia. Imaging: Metaphyseal lucent bands; Symmetric localized demineralization and osseous destruction of medial portion of proximal tibial metaphysis (Wimberger sign); Metaphyseal serration (sawtooth metaphysis, Wegener sign); Diaphyseal periostitis with new bone formation; Irregular areas of increased density and rarefaction (moth-eaten appearance)

parts.text: State the probability of neonatal syphilis in the following scenario: chancre untreated, during pregnancy

cohort_answer.text: 60-90%, primary, untreated

parts.text: State the probability of neonatal syphilis in the following scenario: 1:32 RPR, 14 months before pregnancy, untreated

cohort_answer.text: 10%, late latent, untreated

parts.text: What is Hutchinson's triad?

cohort_answer.text: Triad in late congenital syphilis: notched incisors (malformed teeth); interstitial keratitis (develop age 5-20, typically bilateral); eighth cranial nerve deafness (sensorineural, sudden onset age 8-10)

questions.question: Baby is born with neonatal syphilis (CSF is positive, has snuffles) you decide to give penicillin.

parts.text: Should it be administered IV or IM? Why?

cohort_answer.text: IV penicillin G 50,000 units/kg q12h x 1st 7 days of life, then q8h thereafter, total 10 day course. IV is the formulation of choice for treatment of congenital syphilis because of higher CSF penetration

parts.text: What isolation precautions are indicated for baby with congenital syphilis?

cohort_answer.text: Standard precautions. Cover moist open lesions, secretions, and bodily fluids (infectious) until after 24h of treatment

questions.question:
Q83 (2010 PM)
HIV+ patient with + syphilis serology and develops neurological sequelae

parts.text: A) What investigations would you order from LP?

cohort_answer.text: Cell count and differential; Protein, Glucose; Gram stain, C+S; VDRL (+/- FTA-ABS); Viral (HSV, VZV, enterovirus etc.); Other Ix based on CD4 count (Crypto, toxo, JC etc.)

questions.question:
Q83 (2010 PM)
HIV+ patient with + syphilis serology and develops neurological sequelae

parts.text: B) If patient has anaphylaxis to penicillin, how would you treat?

cohort_answer.text: Desensitize and treat with penicillin (if no way of using PCN at all, can use CEFTRIAXONE)

questions.question:
Q79 (2012 PM)
Secondary syphilis with penicillin anaphylaxis

parts.text: A) 3 reasons to LP in non-HIV

cohort_answer.text: Congenital syphilis; Neurologic sx including ocular/optic; Lack of appropriate RPR response to tx; Tertiary syphilis (gummatous, aortitis)

questions.question:
Q79 (2012 PM)
Secondary syphilis with penicillin anaphylaxis

parts.text: B) 2 treatments including dose?

cohort_answer.text: Ceftriaxone 1g IV/IM daily x10-14 days; Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x14 days (speaker notes: Ceftriaxone, Doxy)

questions.question:
Q79 (2012 PM)
Secondary syphilis with penicillin anaphylaxis

parts.text: C) Followup serology

cohort_answer.text: 3, 6, 12 months - expect 8x drop at 6 months and 16x drop at 12 months (much more dramatic than usual for latent syphilis; these are old Health Canada guidelines). CDC guidelines: 4-fold decline after Rx = cure, 4-fold increase = Rx failure or reinfection; for secondary syphilis likely want to see this within 6-12 months

questions.question:
Q80 (2012 PM)
Syphilis – CMIA +, RPR -, TPPA +

parts.text: A) 4 reasons other than false +

cohort_answer.text: RPR below detection level; Successfully treated syphilis; Early infection (treponemal specific tests become positive earlier); Late latent/tertiary syphilis; Transplacental antibodies in infant; Endemic (non-syphilitic) treponemes (yaws, pinta, bejel) (speaker notes: Late latent, early infection, previously treated, cross-reactivity e.g. lupus)

questions.question:
Q81 (2013 PM)
Syphilis aortitis suspected with + CMIA, TPPA, FTA-Abs and negative RPR

parts.text: C) What other test is indicated?

cohort_answer.text: Lumbar puncture. [Background on tertiary syphilis syndromes given: cardiovascular (aortitis, aneurysms, ascending aorta most affected, linear calcifications of aorta on CXR); gummatous (granuloma-like lesions, skin/mucous membranes/bones); tertiary neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis, general paresis, cerebral atrophy from chronic meningoencephalitis)]

questions.question:
Q82 (2007)
Optic neuritis. A man presents with optic neuritis. VDRL and FTA-ABS are positive

parts.text: A) Additional investigations

cohort_answer.text: LP for CSF cell count, biochemistry and VDRL; Ophthalmologic examination, hearing test; STI screen including HIV

questions.question:
Q84 (2006 AM)
RPR test

parts.text: A) Explain how it works?

cohort_answer.text: Rapid plasma reagin: looks at ability of heat-inactivated serum to flocculate or agglutinate suspension of cardiolipin cholesterol lecithin antigen. Finely divided charcoal particles used for visualization (Mandell's)

questions.question:
Q84 (2006 AM)
RPR test

parts.text: B) List 4 conditions known to cause false positives (but there are many more than 4)

cohort_answer.text: Acute (<6mo): Malaria, Brucellosis, Mononucleosis, Recent smallpox vaccination, Endocarditis, Rickettsial disease. Chronic: SLE in particular, HIV, IVDU, Leprosy, HCV, aging?, pregnancy?, Lyme disease, other treponemes (speaker notes: SLE, Lyme disease, autoimmune disease)

questions.question:
Q84 (2006 AM)
RPR test

parts.text: C) Explain the prozone reaction

cohort_answer.text: Sera with extremely high nontreponemal titers may give weakly reactive or nonreactive results at low dilutions because antibody excess prevents/overwhelms the agglutination reaction. Occurs up to 1% of the time, generally overcome by routinely diluting to at least 16-fold, even when initially negative (Mandell's)

questions.question: Congenital syphilis. Baby asymptomatic.

parts.text: A) Mom treated at 37 weeks IM pen x 1
B) Mom treated early with IM penicillin x 3. RPR 1:64 dropped to 1:2. Baby RPR 1:2
C) Mom treated early 1:32 to 1:2. Baby undetectable

cohort_answer.text:
Because mom was treated within 4 weeks of delivery, considered inadequate. Requires full work up: syphilis serology, LP with cell count/VDRL/protein (as clinically indicated: long bones x-ray, audiology, ophtho). Treat baby with Pen G 50,000U/kg IV q12h x first 7d then q8h for total 10 days
Since mom was treated before 4 weeks from delivery, and baby is asymptomatic, unlikely congenital syphilis. Presumably late latent treatment; baseline and monthly exams for 3 months with serology @0,3,6,18 months. No further assessment unless becomes symptomatic or RPR higher than mom's or does not resolve. RPR should trend down by 3 months, nonreactive at 6 months. Treponemal tests negative by 12-18 months
Over 4-fold decrease in titer and treated early. If no risk of reinfection and titer remains low and baby titer not 4-fold above mom's, do baseline with monthly exams for 3 months and serology @0,3,6,18 months

questions.question: Congenital syphilis

parts.text: How do you make the diagnosis?
Treatment?
C) List 4 clinical situations where you would want to specifically look for congenital syphilis?

cohort_answer.text:
Maternal syphilis screening in first trimester; repeat at 28-32 weeks and delivery if high risk. In CSF always send VDRL not RPR, repeat every 6 mo until negative if initial positive
Maternal: Primary/secondary/early latent - benzathine penicillin G 2.4mU IM x1 dose. Late latent - benzathine pen G 2.4mU IM weekly x3 weeks. Infant: Crystalline penG IV 50,000U/kg q12h x first 7d then q8h for total 10 days
Signs/symptoms present in baby; Abnormal placenta/cord (barber's pole spiral stripes); Mom treated with non-PCN antibiotic; Mom treated within 4 weeks of delivery or inadequately treated; <4 fold titer decline or not documented; Relapse/doubts about adequacy of treatment or reinfection; Adequacy of infant follow-up cannot be assured and mom treated before pregnancy; Stillborn >20 weeks

questions.question: Congenital syphilis: Mom RPR (Non-Treponemal) negative, treponemal test + (EIA), treated with 3 doses of penicillin x 3 weeks. Retested prior to delivery, now RPR is 1:16

parts.text: A) Most likely explanation for negative assay initially
B) What to do for baby?
C) 4 radiographical or lab findings
D) Likelihood of syphilis infections if first or second stage
E) Baby's syphilis serology +, RPR negative. What will you do now, how will you follow?

cohort_answer.text:
Early primary infection - non-treponemal tests become positive 4-6 weeks after infection while treponemal tests become positive earlier and once positive most remain positive despite tx. OR reinfection (consider especially if high risk)
Test baby for RPR/VDRL to ensure titer is 4x less and not greater than mom; infant physical exam. If abnormal to either, baby has proven or highly probable congenital syphilis and treat with PenG x10 days IV. If mom high risk (possible reinfection), full workup with empiric treatment
Lab: CSF abnormalities (pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose); VDRL+ in CSF; Thrombocytopenia; anemia. Radiographic: Symmetrical long bone lesions; Metaphyseal osteochondritis; Wimberger's sign; Diaphyseal periostitis; Osteitis (celery stick appearance); Dactylitis
Vertical transmission depends on maternal stage: Primary/Secondary untreated 70-100% (25% stillbirth, 14% neonatal death, 41% congenital infection, 20% healthy). Early latent 40%. Late latent 10%
Treponemal antibody may remain positive up to 15 months postnatally (maternal Abs), repeat at 18 months should be negative. Repeat RPR at 3 months to rule out incubating congenital syphilis. If positive at all for both, baby warrants tx for congenital syphilis

questions.question: Scenario with woman who had intercourse with patients now diagnosed with secondary syphilis. What to do (investigations and/or treatment) in each of the following scenarios: not pregnant, no allergies; pregnant at 36 weeks; positive RPR at 1:8, pregnant at 36 weeks, and anaphylaxis to PCN; positive RPR, treated at 28 weeks, what to do for baby?

parts.text: Not pregnant, no allergies
Pregnant at 36 weeks
Positive RPR at 1:8, pregnant at 36 weeks, and anaphylaxis to PCN
Positive RPR, treated at 28 weeks, what to do for baby?

cohort_answer.text: Not pregnant/no allergies: Syphilis screen (CMIA for serology, then RPR and TPPA); Rx benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM x1; repeat RPR at 6 months; treat all sexual contacts in past 90 days with 1 dose of benzathine penicillin 2.4mU IM x1. Pregnant at 36 weeks: Syphilis screen and RPR; Rx benzathine pen G 2.4MU IM (1 or 3 doses depending on stage); repeat RPR at 6 months; examine baby (CBC/platelets, CSF cell count/protein/quantitative VDRL, other tests as indicated e.g. CXR, long-bone films, eye exam, LFTs, neuroimaging, ABR). Anaphylaxis to PCN: desensitize to penicillin and give benzathine pen G 2.4MU IM weekly x1-2 doses; repeat RPR at 6 months; examine baby and repeat mom's RPR and do serum/CSF VDRL of baby. Some experts recommend two doses of benzathine penicillin G-LA 2.4 million units one week apart particularly in the third trimester (difficulty staging, pregnancy PK changes, possible benefit). Baby follow-up: examine for abnormalities of congenital syphilis; clinical evaluation at 2,4,6,12 months; repeat RPR at 2-3 months until negative (should decrease by 3 months, negative by 6 months); if baby RPR 4x or more than mom's, proven/highly probable congenital syphilis, treat with 10 days IV pen G; a reactive RPR at 18 months is diagnostic of congenital syphilis (maternal treponemal antibodies can persist until 15 months).

questions.question: PM 11. What is the most likely infectious cause of the following congenital findings? periventricular calcifications (0.5); cutaneous scarring (0.5); heart failure (0.5); Osteitis (0.5); Cataracts (0.5)

parts.text: Identify the infectious cause for each congenital finding

cohort_answer.text: Periventricular calcifications - CMV (widespread/intracranial calcifications more suggest Toxoplasmosis). Cutaneous scarring - VZV. Heart failure - Parvovirus (>>>Rubella). Osteitis - Syphilis (saber shin). Cataracts - Rubella.

questions.question: Congenital infections associated with:

parts.text: Osteitis
Periventricular calcifications
Scarring
Heart failure
Cataracts

questions.model_answer: Congenital infection associations: Osteitis - congenital syphilis (also rubella causing metaphyseal lucencies). Periventricular calcifications - congenital CMV (classically periventricular, vs toxoplasmosis which is diffuse/scattered). Scarring (cutaneous) - congenital varicella syndrome (zigzag cicatricial skin scarring). Heart failure (hydrops) - congenital parvovirus B19 (fetal anemia/hydrops) or CMV myocarditis. Cataracts - congenital rubella syndrome.

parts.text: List 3 causes of genital ulcers in which Doxycycline can be used as a treatment

cohort_answer.text: Syphilis; Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars L1, L2, L3) - lymphogranuloma venereum, first line rx is doxy x21 days; Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis/granuloma inguinale): first line is azithro +/- gent, but doxy or Septra x3 wks are alternative regimens

questions.question:
Q81 (2013 PM)
Syphilis aortitis suspected with + CMIA, TPPA, FTA-Abs and negative RPR

parts.text: A) Explain the serologies in the context of aortitis

cohort_answer.text: Tertiary syphilis. Test sensitivity with nontreponemal tests is lower (71-73%) while high for treponemal specific tests (94-96%). In late syphilis, nontreponemal tests could become nonreactive over time

questions.question: Match the congenital syndrome to the infection: Osteitis, Periventricular calcifications, Scarring (cicatrical), CHF, Cataracts, Dactylitis, Salt and pepper retinopathy, Microcephaly, Hypoplastic lower limbs, Myocarditis

parts.text: Match the congenital syndrome to the infection

cohort_answer.text: Osteitis - Syphilis. Periventricular calcifications - CMV (also Toxo, rubella, HSV, zika). Scarring (cicatrical) - Varicella. Heart failure (congenital heart disease) - Parvovirus B19. Cataracts - Rubella (also syphilis, toxo). Dactylitis - Syphilis (early but rare). Salt and Pepper Retinopathy - Rubella/syphilis. Microcephaly - CMV (most common), rubella, Zika, toxo. Hypoplastic lower limbs - Varicella. Myocarditis - Parvovirus B19, enterovirus D70, Coxsackie A24

questions.question: 16 year old female with perinatally acquired HIV presents for routine follow up. She has positive syphilis serology with RPR 1:8 that was negative 6mo ago (Non-pregnant). She has no symptoms and exam is normal

parts.text: What stage of infection (0.5)
What treatment (drug, dose [Peds didn't ask dose], route, and duration) (0.5)
She is anaphylactic to penicillin. What alternative drug and duration can you use (did not ask dose) (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: Stage: Early latent - asymptomatic with a negative test within 1 year (if no negative test within last year, automatically late latent). Treatment: 1x dose benzathine penicillin 2.4M units, given as 2x1.2M unit doses IM to each buttock. Alternatives: Doxy 100mg PO BID 10-14 days, ceftriaxone 1g IV/IM daily 10-14 days
